extracted.intended_audience: general readers, policymakers, and advocates concerned with free speech and intellectual liberty
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on how opinions and public discussion ought to be treated: why free, open, and robust debate is necessary and what practices/supports are required for opinions to be truly known and valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is not guaranteed to survive persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictum that truth always triumphs over persecution is one of those pleasant falsehoods; history teems with instances of truth put down by persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill gives many historical examples (Reformation suppressed repeatedly; Arnold of Brescia, Fra Dolcino, Savonarola, Albigenses, Vaudois, Lollards, Hussites put down) to show that persecution can and does suppress true opinions for long periods; truth may be extinguished once, twice, or many times until favourable circumstances allow rediscovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: New discoverers of truth must not be punished or martyrized
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who discover and announce new truths render possibly the most precious service and ought not to be requited by martyrdom or treated as criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill criticizes the view (exemplified by Dr. Johnson) that persecution is an appropriate ordeal for truth; he says the doctrine that proposers of new opinions should stand ready for execution (as in Locrian legislation) cannot be commended and reveals contempt for the benefactor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal penalties for opinion or its expression are unjust and dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties for opinion, or at least for its expression, still exist by law and their enforcement shows that legal persecution of opinion is not yet extinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Thomas Pooley sentenced for offensive words about Christianity; George Jacob Holyoake and Edward Truelove and a foreigner rejected or denied justice because of lack of theological belief; the rule excluding non-believers from giving evidence in court effectively makes them outlaws and deprives them of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social stigma can be as effective as law in suppressing opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief mischief of legal penalties is that they strengthen the social stigma; opinion in this respect is as efficacious as law for many people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that exclusion from social means of earning a livelihood or favour has the same chilling effect as imprisonment for those dependent on others; those financially independent have less to fear, but most do face real costs from social ostracism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinions must be fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed or they become dead dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: However true an opinion may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes that true belief held without understanding of its grounds is merely superstition; the value of a truth partly depends on it being subject to continual open examination rather than being accepted from authority alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: One must know the grounds of one's opinions and be able to defend them
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever people believe on subjects of first importance they ought to be able to defend against at least the common objections; knowledge of grounds is essential to cultivate intellect and judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts mathematics (where all argument is on one side) with moral, religious, political subjects where every point depends on showing why alternative explanations are not true; Mill argues that instruction should enable people to understand and defend beliefs, not merely parrot them from authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with opponents' arguments in their strongest, most persuasive form
rubrics_metrics.description: One must hear opposing arguments from persons who actually believe them, defended in earnest and in their most plausible and persuasive form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill invokes Cicero's practice of studying the adversary's case thoroughly and recommends acting as a devil's advocate where real opponents do not exist; the intellectual discipline of fairly representing and confronting opposing views is necessary to 'possess' the truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free and daring speculation fosters general intellectual vitality and social progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom to dispute principles and engage in heterodox speculation is indispensable to produce an intellectually active people and to generate the major improvements in mind and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites three historical periods (post-Reformation, late-18th-century speculative movement on the Continent, the Goethian/Fichtean period in Germany) where breaking the yoke of authority produced lasting improvements; without such freedom, only isolated great thinkers may arise but not an active, thinking populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of debate harms non-heretics and curtails mental development
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest harm of banning inquiry is to those who are not heretics: their whole mental development is cramped and their reason cowed by fear of heresy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill describes timid promising intellects who dare not pursue independent thought, or who sophisticate to reconcile conscience with orthodoxy; the loss to society includes many thinking persons who never reach full intellectual maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief formation requires weighing conflicting reasons; absence of real opponents requires imagined ones
rubrics_metrics.description: On subjects where difference of opinion is possible, truth depends on a balance struck between two sets of conflicting reasons; if real opponents do not exist, it is indispensable to imagine them and supply the strongest arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill gives scientific analogies (geocentric vs heliocentric; phlogiston vs oxygen) and insists that understanding requires knowing how alternate theories could claim the facts; without contestation one cannot see the decisive parts of truth that swing judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment of opinion presupposes an unjust claim to infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who approve punishment for promulgation of opinions flatter themselves that they, together with the multitude, possess a joint infallibility greater than even the wisest past figures (e.g., Marcus Aurelius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Marcus Aurelius as an example, Mill argues that defenders of punitive suppression must implicitly claim superior wisdom or virtue to justify silencing others; this is an arrogant and untenable assumption.
